periods.activity_title: Consecutive-Square Patterns and the Promise of Algebraic Identities
periods.visual_aids: Board table showing three sets of consecutive squares and the computed invariant

textbook_items_in_class.description: Demonstrates that for three consecutive square numbers, adding the smallest and largest and subtracting twice the middle square always gives 2, checked with two numeric sets.

time_bands.activity: Invite students to choose any two sets of three consecutive integers and compute the squares. Ask: what do you notice when you add the first and third squares and subtract twice the second? Record results on the board and let students conjecture the invariant.
Work through Example 1, p.68 together, verifying the invariant for two numeric sets shown in the textbook. Ask students to test one further set of their own choice and confirm the pattern holds.

Pose the think-and-reflect prompt from section 4.1: can students find a similar invariant for four consecutive squares? Let students work in pairs, compute, and share conjectures with the class. Discuss why a purely numeric test cannot constitute proof.

Close by having students write, in their own words, why the numeric pattern is surprising and what kind of argument would convince them it always holds. Collect one sentence per student as an exit reflection.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter by letting the numeric surprise do the motivating work — no algebraic machinery is needed yet, and students should feel free to conjecture. Watch for students who assume that verifying three or four cases proves the result; use the think-reflect discussion to draw out the distinction between evidence and proof. Example 1, p.68 is straightforward and can be revisited at home by students who want further numeric confirmation.

periods.activity_title: Building and Proving the Binomial-Square Identity Geometrically
materials: Ruler and pencil for sketching partitioned squares
periods.visual_aids: Partitioned square of side (a+b) showing four sub-regions labelled a², ab, ab, b²

textbook_items_in_class.description: Verifies (a+b)^2 = a^2+2ab+b^2 for negative values a=-2, b=-3.
Expands (5x+2y)^2 using the identity (a+b)^2 = a^2+2ab+b^2.
Computes 43^2 as (40+3)^2 using the identity.

time_bands.activity: Draw the square of side (a+b) on the board and guide students to partition it into four regions. Label each region and read off the area sum, establishing (a+b)² = a² + 2ab + b² from the geometric picture. Then prove the same result algebraically using the distributive property, step by step.

Work through Example 2, p.70 (negative values) and Example 3, p.71 (binomial with coefficients) to show the identity holds for any real a, b. Emphasise matching the pattern: identify a and b explicitly before expanding.

Work through Example 4, p.71: compute 43² = (40+3)² as a class. Then pose the think-and-reflect prompt: compare (a+b)² and a²+b² — when is each larger, and when are they equal? Let students work individually, then discuss.
Students attempt Exercise 4.1 Q1 (i)–(iii) from p.71 independently. Select two contrasting expansions to present at the board and invite the class to spot any pattern or error in the working shown.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established the consecutive-square pattern numerically, this unit gives students the algebraic engine that will explain it. The most common error here is writing (a+b)² = a² + b², which the think-and-reflect discussion directly addresses — use the geometric picture to make the missing 2ab visible. Students who finish early can read Example 4, p.71 again and try a second numerical square such as 97² = (100-3)² on their own to preview the coming unit.
homework: Complete Exercise 4.1 Q1 (iv)–(vi), p.71, showing full working for each expansion.

periods.activity_title: Factorising Perfect-Square Trinomials and the Difference-of-Squares Identity

textbook_items_in_class.description: Factors x^2+4x+4 as (x+2)^2 by matching it to a^2+2ab+b^2.
Factors 36x^2+12x+1 as (6x+1)^2.
Factors 50p^2+60pq+18q^2 by first extracting a common factor of 2, then matching the remainder to the square identity to get 2(5p+3q)^2.
Computes 29^2 as (30-1)^2 using the identity (a-b)^2 = a^2-2ab+b^2.
Factor completely four quadratic expressions (i)-(iv) using the perfect-square identity (asterisked parts (v)-(vi) excluded).
Find the values of (79)^2, (193)^2, (299)^2 using (a-b)^2 = a^2-2ab+b^2.

time_bands.activity: Frame the reverse problem: given a trinomial, can we recognise it as a perfect square? Walk through Examples 5 and 6 (pp.72) together — identify a and b by inspecting the first and last terms, verify the middle term, and write the factored form.

Work through Example 7, p.72 to show that a common factor must be extracted first. Then introduce (a-b)² = a²-2ab+b² by substituting -b for b in the expansion already proved, and apply it via Example 8, p.73 to compute 29².
Students work in pairs on Exercise 4.2 Q1 (i)–(iv) from p.74. After six minutes of independent work, pairs compare answers and resolve any disagreement before a whole-class check.

Prove the consecutive-square pattern from section 4.1 algebraically: let the three consecutive integers be n-1, n, n+1, expand (n-1)² and (n+1)² using the identities, and show the expression equals 2. Then ask students to attempt Exercise 4.2 Q2, p.75 as a quick individual calculation.

periods.teacher_notes: Having derived (a+b)², this unit runs the identity in reverse and introduces its companion. A common error is misidentifying b in the middle term — students sometimes write 12x as 2·(6x)·1 and correctly get b=1, but then forget to check that the last term matches b²; insist on the three-way check. Example 8, p.73 is a good self-study item for students to revisit when practising numerical applications of (a-b)².
homework: Exercise 4.2 Q2, p.75 — find (79)², (193)², (299)² showing the (a-b)² decomposition explicitly.

periods.activity_title: Extending to Three Terms: Deriving and Applying (a+b+c)²
materials: Coloured chalk or markers for geometric figure
periods.visual_aids: Partitioned square of side (a+b+c) showing nine sub-regions with labels

textbook_items_in_class.description: Computes 119^2 as (100+10+9)^2 using the three-term square identity.
Find six squares (117^2, 78^2, 198^2, 214^2, 1104^2, 1120^2), choosing the more convenient identity for each.
Expand (p+3q+7r)^2 and (3x-2y+4z)^2 using the three-term square identity.

time_bands.activity: Derive (a+b+c)² by substituting d = b+c into the two-variable identity: (a+d)² = a²+2ad+d², then expand d² = (b+c)² and collect terms. Write out each step slowly and have students verify each line. Show the corresponding geometric figure with nine labelled sub-regions.

Work through Example 9, p.76: decompose 119 as 100+10+9 and apply the identity. Address the think-and-reflect prompt on labelling the geometric figure — ask a volunteer to come up and label the nine sub-regions of the board diagram correctly.

Students attempt Exercise 4.3 Q1, p.76 (at least three of the six squares) individually, choosing the most convenient identity for each. Discuss: why is 78² more conveniently done as (80-2)² than as a three-term split?

Students work through Exercise 4.3 Q3, p.77 (expand (p+3q+7r)² and (3x-2y+4z)²) in pairs, paying attention to signs when a term is negative. One pair presents each expansion on the board for checking.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established the two-variable square identities, this unit extends the method by a single substitution step — the derivation is short but the result is dense with cross-terms. The most common error is forgetting the cross-terms 2ab, 2bc, and 2ca, especially 2ca which students often skip last. Exercise 4.3 Q3, p.77 is a useful self-study item for students who want extra practice with the three-term form including negative coefficients.
homework: Exercise 4.3 Q2, p.77 — factor the five expressions using suitable identities.

periods.activity_title: Algebra Tiles: Representing Quadratic Products and Splitting the Middle Term
materials: Paper cut-outs or drawn tiles representing x²-tile, x-tile, unit tile
periods.visual_aids: Tile rectangle diagram showing (x+3)(x+4) = x²+7x+12 with labelled rows and columns

time_bands.activity: Introduce the algebra-tile model from section 4.5: each tile type represents a monomial. Demonstrate building a rectangle whose area is (x+3)(x+4) — place the x²-tile, then the x-strips in two groups (3 and 4), then the 12 unit tiles. Count the total area tile by tile: x²+7x+12.

Ask students: the 7x in the middle came from 3x+4x — can it come from 2x+5x instead? Use the think-and-reflect prompt directly: try to build a valid rectangle with that split. Let students attempt this with drawn tiles and report back whether a complete rectangle is possible.

Extend to the two-variable case: draw the tile rectangle for (2x+3)(3x+1) on the board and have students identify the four types of tiles (x², x, and unit tiles in two colours if available). Read off the product as 6x²+11x+3, connecting each tile area to the distributed terms.
Students sketch their own tile rectangle for a product of their choice (e.g. (x+5)(x+2)) and write the expanded form beneath. Pairs exchange and check each other's tile diagrams for completeness.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit uses the visual/physical tile model before the symbolic procedure so that the splitting of the middle term has a concrete referent. The key insight from the think-and-reflect is that only one split of the middle term produces a valid rectangular array — this is what makes factorisation determinate. Watch for students who arrange tiles in a non-rectangular L-shape and claim the product is valid; insist that the arrangement must close into a rectangle.

periods.activity_title: Middle-Term Splitting Without Tiles: Factorising General Quadratics

textbook_items_in_class.description: Factors x^2+7x+12 by finding a,b with a+b=7 and ab=12, giving (x+3)(x+4).
Factors x^2+11x+30 by finding a,b with a+b=11 and ab=30, giving (x+5)(x+6).
Factors x^2-5x+6 by finding negative a,b with a+b=-5 and ab=6.
Fill in the blanks to complete four factorisation identities (i)-(iv), including splitting the middle term of quadratics with leading coefficient other than 1.
Factor five algebraic expressions (i)-(v) using identities, including three-variable square-type expressions.

time_bands.activity: State the method formally: to factorise x²+(a+b)x+ab, find two numbers whose sum is the coefficient of x and whose product is the constant term. Work through Example 10, p.81 step by step, listing factor pairs of 12 and selecting the pair that sums to 7.

Work through Example 11, p.81 (x²+11x+30) and then Example 12, p.81 (x²-5x+6) to handle the negative-coefficient case. Emphasise that both a and b must be negative when the product is positive and the sum is negative — this is the classic sign-error trap.

Students work individually on Exercise 4.4 Q1, p.81 (fill in the blanks). After a quick whole-class check, move to Exercise 4.4 Q3, p.82 in pairs, factorising expressions including any with negative or larger coefficients.

Pose the think-and-reflect debate from section 4.6: two students derive (a-b)²(a+b) by different routes — which is correct? Students judge and explain in one sentence. Optionally, those who finish early attempt End of Chapter Q8, p.90.

periods.teacher_notes: Having seen middle-term splitting via the tile model, students now formalise the algebraic procedure. The most persistent error is sign confusion when both factors are negative — reinforce the double check: verify that the product of the two chosen numbers equals the constant term AND their sum equals the coefficient. Example 12, p.81 is the key self-study item for students who struggle with the negative-coefficient case.
homework: Exercise 4.4 Q2, p.81 — use suitable identities to compute the eight products/squares without direct multiplication.

periods.activity_title: Proving the Difference of Squares and Verifying Identities

textbook_items_in_class.description: Factor five expressions using suitable identities (i)-(v).
Determine whether (a+b-c)^2+(a-b+c)^2+(a-b-c)^2 = 2a^2+2b^2+2c^2 is an identity.
Use suitable identities to find nine products/expansions (i)-(ix), including binomial squares, difference-of-squares, and a binomial cube.

time_bands.activity: Derive a²-b² = (a+b)(a-b) by expanding the right side using the distributive property, then confirm by substituting small values. Discuss: why does this not appear in the section alongside (a+b)² and (a-b)²? Use Exercise 4.3 Q2, p.77 (i)–(ii) to apply the difference-of-squares identity in factorisation.

Work through Exercise 4.3 Q4, p.77 as a whole class: expand each squared trinomial on the left using the three-term identity and simplify, checking whether the equality reduces to a true statement for all values of a, b, c. This is practice in the identity-verification technique.

Students attempt End of Chapter Q1, p.88 (i)–(vi) in pairs — the question spans binomial squares, three-term squares, and difference-of-squares. After each pair completes three parts, they swap to check a neighbour's working.

Quick whole-class discussion: which parts of Q1 required the three-term identity rather than the two-term identity? Students articulate the decision rule — three addends require the three-term form — in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit consolidates section 4.4 by introducing the difference-of-squares identity and practising identity verification — two skills that also underpin the simplification of rational expressions. A common error in the verification task (Exercise 4.3 Q4) is expanding only two of the three squared brackets; insist that all three must be expanded and collected before a verdict is possible. End of Chapter Q1, p.88 (vii)–(ix) involve cube identities and may be set for self-study by students who have already met the cube identities.
homework: End of Chapter Q1, p.88 — complete any remaining parts (vii)–(ix), which draw on the cube identities.

periods.activity_title: Deriving the Binomial-Cube Identities and Their Geometric Interpretation
materials: Optional: physical wooden or cardboard cube cut into 8 pieces
periods.visual_aids: Decomposition diagram of a cube of edge (a+b) into two cubes and six rectangular cuboids

textbook_items_in_class.description: Finds the cube root of p^3+6p^2q+12pq^2+8q^3 by matching it to (a+b)^3, giving side p+2q.
Finds the cube root of 8n^3-60n^2m+150nm^2-125m^3 by matching it to (a-b)^3, giving 2n-5m.

time_bands.activity: Derive (a+b)³ = a³+3a²b+3ab²+b³ by distributing (a+b)² · (a+b) step by step. Then show the geometric interpretation: a cube of edge (a+b) decomposes into two smaller cubes (edges a and b) and six rectangular cuboids (two of each of the three distinct dimensions). Verify the volume sum equals the algebraic expansion.
Derive (a-b)³ by substituting -b for b in the result just proved, carrying the signs carefully. Write both identities side by side and highlight the sign alternation pattern.

Work through Example 13, p.84 and Example 14, p.84 as a class: identify a and b by inspecting the first and last terms, verify the coefficients of the middle terms match, then state the cube root. Students attempt a quick individual variation.

Introduce the think-and-reflect from section 4.7: does (x-y) remain a factor as the exponent increases? Students test x⁴-y⁴ by factoring (x²-y²)² — no, use (x²)²-(y²)² — and discuss. Record the conjecture: (x-y) divides xⁿ-yⁿ for all positive integer n.

periods.teacher_notes: The geometric decomposition of the cube is visually rich but the algebra that follows it is dense — work slowly through the sign patterns. The most common error when applying (a-b)³ is treating the 3ab² term as negative; stress that (-b)² = b² is positive, so only the terms with an odd power of b are negative. Example 14, p.84 is worth revisiting independently as a self-study item for students who find the coefficient-matching step for (a-b)³ slippery.
homework: End of Chapter Q2, p.89 (i)–(iii): find 17×21, 104×96, 24×16 using the difference-of-squares identity.

periods.activity_title: Sum and Difference of Cubes, and the Three-Variable Cube Identity

textbook_items_in_class.description: Uses the identity x^3+y^3+z^3-3xyz = (x+y+z)(x^2+y^2+z^2-xy-xz-yz) to find the sum of cubes of three numbers given their sum, product, and sum of squares.
Find eight values using suitable identities: 17x21, 104x96, 24x16, 147^3, 199^3, 127^3, (-107)^3, (-299)^3.
Factor eleven algebraic expressions (i)-(xi) using the chapter's identities, including sum/difference-of-cubes and three-term-cube forms.

time_bands.activity: Derive x³-y³ = (x-y)(x²+xy+y²) by expanding the right side and verifying cancellation. Then substitute -y for y to obtain x³+y³ = (x+y)(x²-xy+y²). Write both results together and note the sign difference in the quadratic factor.

Present the identity x³+y³+z³-3xyz = (x+y+z)(x²+y²+z²-xy-xz-yz) without full derivation — verify it for small integers as a class, then state that it follows from combining the cube expansion and the three-term square identity. Work through Example 15, p.85.

Students attempt End of Chapter Q2, p.89 (iv)–(viii) (the cube computations: 147³, 199³, 127³, etc.) using the binomial-cube identities. After individual work, a student presents one computation at the board with full working.
Brief preview of End of Chapter Q3, p.89: read out two of the eleven expressions and ask students to identify by inspection which identity applies. Record their identifications.

periods.teacher_notes: Having derived the binomial-cube identities, this unit derives the sum- and difference-of-cubes and the three-variable form. The most common error is confusing the sign in the quadratic factor: x³-y³ gives (x-y)(x²+xy+y²) where all three terms inside the bracket are positive, while x³+y³ gives (x+y)(x²-xy+y²) where the middle term is negative. Example 15, p.85 is useful self-study for students who want further practice with the three-variable identity.
homework: End of Chapter Q3, p.89 — attempt any four of the eleven factorisation problems, choosing at least one from the sum/difference-of-cubes family.

periods.activity_title: Simplifying Rational Expressions by Factorisation and Cancellation

textbook_items_in_class.description: Simplifies the rational expression (x^2-7x+12)/(5x^2+5x-100) by factoring numerator and denominator and cancelling the common factor (x-4).
Finds the length and breadth of a rectangle built from a square of side x, eight x-by-1 strips, and fifteen unit squares by factoring x^2+8x+15.
Simplify six rational expressions (i)-(vi) by factoring numerator and denominator and cancelling common non-zero factors.

time_bands.activity: Explain the simplification procedure for rational algebraic expressions: factorise numerator and denominator separately using the identities developed in earlier sections, identify common factors, and cancel — with the explicit condition that the cancelled factor is non-zero. Work through Example 16, p.86 step by step.

Work through Example 17, p.87: use the tile-model description to set up x²+8x+15 and factor it to find the rectangle's dimensions. Discuss why the problem requires factorisation rather than direct measurement.
Students work individually on Exercise 4.5 Q1, p.87 (i)–(iv). After individual work, pairs compare and resolve any disagreements, then a brief whole-class check covers the trickier parts.

Pose the think-and-reflect from section 4.8: ask students to simplify a fresh rational expression by first factoring its quadratic denominator — they set it up and identify the common factor, without completing the full simplification, to practise the set-up step.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit brings all the factorisation tools to bear on rational expression simplification — the procedure is short but demands fluency in the underlying identities. The most common error is cancelling individual terms rather than factors (e.g. cancelling x from the numerator and denominator independently when x is not a common factor of the whole numerator); use Example 16, p.86 to show explicitly that only a common factor of the whole numerator and denominator may be cancelled. Exercise 4.5 Q1 (v)–(vi), p.87 are good self-study items for students who want to practise with higher-degree expressions.
homework: Exercise 4.5 Q1, p.87 — complete parts (v)–(vi) showing both the factored forms before cancellation.

periods.activity_title: Applied Problems: Rectangles, Pools, and Factorisation in Context

textbook_items_in_class.description: Finds the length and breadth of a rectangular pool of area 96 sq. m where breadth is 4 m less than length, by factoring x^2-4x-96=0.
Simplify three rational expressions (i)-(iii) using factorisation by identities.
Find a number which, when added to its reciprocal, equals 10/3.
Find the length of a rectangular pool of area 2x^2+7x+3 sq. hastas given its width is 2x+1 hastas.

time_bands.activity: Work through Example 18, p.88 as a class: set up the quadratic equation from the area condition, rearrange to standard form x²-4x-96=0, and apply middle-term splitting to factor and solve. Verify that the positive root gives a sensible length.
Students work in pairs on End of Chapter Q8 and Q9 (pp.90) — both require translating a word problem into a quadratic and factorising. Each pair writes the set-up equation before factorising.

Work through End of Chapter Q4, p.89 (i)–(ii) together: these rational-expression simplifications require cube and difference-of-squares identities in the denominator, so rehearse the factorisation step before cancelling.

Quick consolidation: students write down, without the textbook, the standard procedure for solving a word problem that leads to a quadratic — set up, standard form, split middle term, solve, interpret. Collect as an exit slip.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit extends section 4.8 to worded problems that require constructing the quadratic before factorising — a higher demand than rational-expression simplification. A common error is accepting both roots of the quadratic without checking physical sense; for a length, only the positive root is admissible. End of Chapter Q4, p.89 (iii) involves a sum-of-cubes in the numerator and is a strong self-study item for students ready for an additional challenge.
homework: End of Chapter Q5, p.89 — find possible length and breadth expressions for the two rectangles given their area expressions.

periods.activity_title: Consolidating Identities: Factorisation, Rational Expressions, and Cross-Chapter Applications

textbook_items_in_class.description: Factor eleven algebraic expressions (i)-(xi) using the chapter's identities, including sum/difference-of-cubes and three-term-cube forms.
Find possible length and breadth expressions for two rectangles given their area expressions (i)-(ii).
Find possible length, breadth, and height expressions for two cuboids given their volume expressions (i)-(ii).
Find an expression in terms of s for the area of a walking path of width s around a square playground of side 40 m.

time_bands.activity: Organise students into groups of three. Each group is assigned two expressions from End of Chapter Q3, p.89 (drawn from the full set of eleven) to factorise, identifying which identity applies and showing full working. Groups then present their solutions at the board.

Work through End of Chapter Q5, p.89 and Q6, p.89 as a class discussion: recovering dimensions from an area or volume expression requires factorising and then interpreting the factors geometrically. Emphasise that both factors must be polynomials with positive leading coefficients for length/dimension meaning.

Students work individually on End of Chapter Q7, p.90 (walking-path area in terms of s). After setting up and simplifying, students compare with a neighbour to check agreement, then extend: what if the playground had side 50 m and path width t — write the new expression.

Pose a synthesis question drawn from section 4.6 and 4.8: given that x²+px+q simplifies a rational expression, what must p and q satisfy? Students conjecture and justify their answer using the sum-and-product conditions from middle-term splitting. Collect responses as an exit check.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws on the factorisation work from sections 4.6, 4.7, and 4.8 to consolidate across the chapter's end-of-chapter problems — a natural place for a unit that advances coverage of these problems without revisiting any section as mere review. Watch for students who in Q3 of End of Chapter blindly try perfect-square trinomials on cube expressions; the think-and-reflect prompt from section 4.7 about (x-y) as a repeating factor can help orient them. End of Chapter Q6 (ii), p.89 requires a common factor extraction before middle-term splitting, a two-step pattern worth dwelling on with the group that presents it.
homework: End of Chapter Q6, p.89 — find possible length, breadth, and height expressions for both cuboids, showing all factorisation steps.

implied_lo: Students can verify the consecutive-square invariant numerically and articulate why algebraic proof is needed beyond numerical evidence.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Consecutive-square numeric pattern, invariant equals 2, motivation for identities

implied_lo: Students can expand a binomial square (a+b)² = a²+2ab+b² using the geometric partition and the distributive property, and apply it to compute squares of numbers and binomial expressions.
Students can compare (a+b)² and a²+b² and determine when they are equal.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Geometric square partition into four regions, distributive-property proof, numerical application

coverage_handoff.section_title: Factorisation of Algebraic Expressions Using Identities
implied_lo: Students can factorise perfect-square trinomials of the form a²±2ab+b² by matching coefficients, including when a common factor must first be extracted.
Students can apply (a-b)² = a²-2ab+b² to compute squares of numbers and prove the consecutive-square pattern algebraically.

questions.question_text: Three consecutive integers are chosen: 6, 7, and 8. Their squares are 36, 49, and 64. When you add the smallest and largest squares and subtract twice the middle square, the result is 2. Which statement best explains why this result is always 2 for any three consecutive integers, not just 6, 7, 8?

options.label: A
options.text: Because consecutive squares grow at an even rate, the differences always cancel to give the same small number.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the middle integer is always the average of the other two, its square is always the average of the other two squares.

options.label: C
options.text: Letting the three integers be n−1, n, n+1, the expression (n−1)²+( n+1)²−2n² simplifies algebraically to 2 for every value of n.

options.label: D
options.text: The pattern holds only for integers where the middle square is a multiple of 7; we happened to choose such a set.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses an informal observation about growth rates with a proof; does not identify the algebraic mechanism.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Applies the arithmetic-mean idea correctly but incorrectly extends it to squares — the square of the mean is not the mean of the squares (Jensen's inequality direction).
what_each_option_reveals.D: Attributes the invariant to a special numerical property of the specific set chosen, showing no understanding that the result is universal.

MCQ.inclusivity: For students who find the symbolic argument abstract, ask them first to test four or five sets of consecutive integers and record the result, then ask what would change if they used n instead of 7. For students ready for a challenge, ask them to modify the expression — what does (n−1)²+(n+1)²−2n²+4 always equal, and can they predict without computing?

questions.question_text: Use the identity (a+b)² = a²+2ab+b² to compute the value of (3x + 5y)² when x = 2 and y = 1. Show all working, including the expanded algebraic form before substituting the values.
questions.method_one_line: Expand (3x+5y)² = 9x²+30xy+25y² by the identity, then substitute x=2, y=1 to get 9(4)+30(2)+25(1) = 36+60+25 = 121.

NUM.inclusivity: For students who struggle with two-variable binomials, begin with a = 3x, b = 5y as literal substitution labels before expanding. For students who finish quickly, ask them to compute (3x+5y)² − (3x)² − (5y)² and explain geometrically what this quantity represents.

questions.question_text: For real numbers a and b, the identity (a+b)² = a²+2ab+b² shows that (a+b)² and a²+b² are equal only in one specific situation. Which situation makes (a+b)² = a²+b² true?

options.label: C
options.text: When at least one of a or b is zero

options.label: D
options.text: When a and b are both negative

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the condition for equality of a and b with the condition that makes 2ab vanish; when a = b, 2ab = 2a² ≠ 0 in general.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Correctly identifies a case where ab = 0 is not satisfied (a = −b gives ab = −a², not zero) — however, note that when a = −b, a+b = 0 so (a+b)² = 0 while a²+b² = 2a²; they are equal only if a = 0 too, reducing to option C.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Both negative: ab is positive, so 2ab > 0 and (a+b)² > a²+b²; the sign of both values does not make 2ab vanish.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the algebra abstract can substitute pairs of numbers for each option and test numerically before reasoning generally. Students ready for a challenge can show algebraically that (a+b)² ≥ a²+b² for all real a, b, with equality iff ab = 0.

questions.question_text: Factorise completely: 75m² − 90mn + 27n². Show all steps, including any common factor extracted before matching the perfect-square identity.
questions.method_one_line: Extract the common factor 3 to get 3(25m²−30mn+9n²), recognise 25m²−30mn+9n² = (5m)²−2(5m)(3n)+(3n)² = (5m−3n)², giving 3(5m−3n)².

NUM.inclusivity: Students who struggle to identify the common factor can first list the GCD of 75, 90, and 27 using prime factorisation as a support step. Students who finish quickly can verify their answer by expanding 3(5m−3n)² and checking it matches the original expression term by term.

questions.question_text: Prove algebraically that for any integer n, the expression (n−1)² + (n+1)² − 2n² always equals 2. In your proof, state which identity you are using at each step, and explain why the result is 2 and not a different constant.
look_for: Expands (n−1)² using (a−b)² = a²−2ab+b² to get n²−2n+1.
Expands (n+1)² using (a+b)² = a²+2ab+b² to get n²+2n+1.
Adds the two expansions and subtracts 2n²: (n²−2n+1)+(n²+2n+1)−2n² = 2n²+2−2n² = 2.
Names both identities explicitly (or derives them from the distributive property).
Explains why the n² and ±2n terms cancel, leaving only the constant terms 1+1 = 2.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find the general proof difficult can first verify the result for n = 5 and n = 10, then write n in place of 5 and observe what changes. Students ready for an extension can investigate whether the analogous expression for four consecutive integers, (n−1)²+(n+2)²−(n)²−(n+1)², is also constant, and prove or disprove it.

questions.question_text: Which of the following expressions is correctly factorised using the difference-of-squares identity a²−b² = (a+b)(a−b)?

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the difference-of-squares factorisation with the perfect-square trinomial; (2x−3)² = 4x²−12x+9, which is not 4x²−9.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Arrives at a factorisation that expands to 4x²−12x−9x+27, not 4x²−9; shows an error in matching factors to the original expression.

questions.question_text: A student wants to use algebra tiles to find the factors of x²+9x+20. She places one x²-tile, nine x-tiles, and twenty unit tiles. She says: 'I can split the 9 x-tiles as 4 x-tiles and 5 x-tiles to form a complete rectangle.' (a) Show the dimensions of the rectangle she forms and write down the factorisation. (b) Explain, in one or two sentences, why splitting the 9 x-tiles as 3 and 6 would NOT give a valid rectangular tile arrangement.
expected_elements: Identifies the rectangle as having dimensions (x+4) and (x+5), giving x²+9x+20 = (x+4)(x+5).
Explains that a 3–6 split would require 3×6 = 18 unit tiles to fill the corner, but 20 unit tiles are available — the rectangle does not close (or equivalently, 3 and 6 have product 18 ≠ 20).

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find drawing the tile rectangle abstract can describe it in words — list the tile types in each row and column — rather than sketching. Students ready for more can investigate a third split (e.g. 1x+8x) and explain why that too fails.

competency.competency_text: Apply one repeatable procedure — middle-term splitting — across several differently-signed quadratics to factorise them.

questions.task:
Below are four quadratic expressions. For each one, use the middle-term splitting method to factorise it completely. Show all steps: (a) state the two numbers whose sum and product match the coefficients, (b) rewrite the middle term as two terms, (c) group and factorise, and (d) write the final factored form.

(i) x² + 8x + 15
(ii) x² − 7x + 12
(iii) x² + 2x − 15
(iv) x² − x − 12

After factorising all four, answer: What pattern do you notice about the signs of the two numbers when the constant term (q) is positive versus negative? Write your observation as a rule.
questions.scaffold: For each expression, begin by listing all integer factor-pairs of the constant term q (positive and negative pairs). Then identify the pair whose sum equals p. Split the middle term using that pair, then group the four terms into two pairs and extract a common factor from each pair.
format_of_output: Four complete factorisations with working (sum and product conditions stated for each).
A written sign-rule observation: one or two sentences describing when both factors share a sign and when they differ.

OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The implied LO is the repeated application of one procedure across four differently-signed quadratics culminating in a generalisation — a procedure-and-pattern task that naturally calls for multi-case working followed by a written rule. The teacher may substitute any other format from the Mathematics open-task menu.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student demonstrates fluency in middle-term splitting across all sign combinations of the coefficient p and constant q, and the ability to abstract a sign-rule from the four cases.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold directs the student to list factor pairs systematically before selecting — this prevents trial-and-error guessing and models the structured procedure the section develops. The final sign-rule question is open: any correct observation about the relationship between the sign of q and the signs of the two chosen numbers is acceptable.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: all four factorisations correct with sum and product conditions explicitly stated; sign-rule is precise (e.g. 'when q > 0 both numbers share the sign of p; when q < 0 the numbers have opposite signs'). Weak: one or more factorisations missing or with sign errors; sign-rule absent or vague ('sometimes both are negative').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle with negative factor pairs can use a factor-pair table (two columns: factor 1, factor 2; rows for all pairs of the constant). Students who finish all four and the rule quickly can investigate whether the same sign-rule holds when the leading coefficient is not 1, using 2x²+7x+3 as a test case.

questions.question_text: Find the cube root of the polynomial expression 27a³ − 108a²b + 144ab² − 64b³ by matching it to the identity (x−y)³ = x³−3x²y+3xy²−y³. Show how you identify x and y, verify the middle coefficients, and state the cube root.
questions.method_one_line: Set x³ = 27a³ so x = 3a, and y³ = 64b³ so y = 4b; verify 3x²y = 3(9a²)(4b) = 108a²b and 3xy² = 3(3a)(16b²) = 144ab² — both match; cube root is 3a−4b.

NUM.inclusivity: Students who find the coefficient matching difficult can be encouraged to first write out the general form (x−y)³ symbolically and then place boxes where x and y appear, filling in from the first and last terms before checking the middle. Students who finish quickly can expand (3a−4b)³ fully and verify it matches the given polynomial term by term.

questions.question_text: Two students are asked to factorise x³+y³. Arjun writes: x³+y³ = (x+y)³ − 3xy(x+y), so x³+y³ = (x+y)[(x+y)²−3xy]. Priya writes: x³+y³ = (x+y)(x²−xy+y²) by the sum-of-cubes identity. Judge which approach is correct. If both are algebraically valid, show that the two factored forms are equivalent. If one contains an error, identify it precisely and correct it.
look_for: Recognises that Arjun's approach uses the cube expansion rearranged: (x+y)³ = x³+3x²y+3xy²+y³ implies x³+y³ = (x+y)³−3xy(x+y), which is correct.
Recognises Priya's factorisation as the direct sum-of-cubes identity, also correct.
Concludes both forms are equivalent and correctly derived.
Awards credit for explaining WHY the cross-term 2xy−3xy = −xy produces the −xy term in the standard factorisation.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain about Arjun's step can be asked to first expand (x+y)³ fully and then isolate x³+y³ on one side — this concretises the rearrangement. Students ready for an additional challenge can attempt to derive an analogous two-form factorisation of x³−y³ and verify equivalence.

questions.question_text: Simplify the rational expression (x²−16) / (x²+x−20). Show the factored forms of both the numerator and the denominator before cancelling, and state the condition on x for which the cancellation is valid.
questions.method_one_line: Factor numerator as (x+4)(x−4) using difference of squares; factor denominator as (x+5)(x−4) using middle-term splitting (sum=1, product=−20); cancel (x−4) for x≠4, giving (x+4)/(x+5) with x≠−5 also excluded.

NUM.inclusivity: Students who are unsure which identity to use for the numerator can be prompted to check whether it fits a²−b² by asking 'Is 16 a perfect square?' For the denominator they can list factor pairs of −20 as a table. Students who finish quickly can substitute x=2 into both the original and simplified expressions and verify they give the same value.

questions.question_text: A rectangular courtyard has an area of 48 square metres. Its length is 2 metres more than its breadth. Set up a quadratic equation in terms of the breadth x, factorise it using the middle-term splitting method, and find the length and breadth. Show all steps and reject any root that is not physically meaningful.
questions.method_one_line: Let breadth = x, then length = x+2; area gives x(x+2) = 48, so x²+2x−48 = 0; split middle term using numbers −6 and 8 (sum=2, product=−48): x²+8x−6x−48 = x(x+8)−6(x+8) = (x−6)(x+8) = 0; x=6 (reject x=−8 as length cannot be negative); breadth=6, length=8.

NUM.inclusivity: Students who struggle with setting up the equation can be asked to draw a labelled rectangle with breadth x and length x+2 and write the area formula before forming the quadratic. Students who finish quickly can verify by computing 6×8 = 48 and then ask: if the area were 60 square metres instead, would the same method work — and attempt it.
